source.title: Looped Uniform Diffusion Language Models
source.authors: Saiteja Utpala; Chieh-Hsin Lai; Yuki Mitsufuji; Praneeth Vepakomma

page_placements.theme: Weight sharing, recurrence and parallel streams add computation beyond stored parameters

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies recurrent computation in uniform diffusion language models, not scaling-law fits or compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. It cites Kaplan and Hoffmann and uses their FLOP-counting conventions, but does not test the claimed laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports validation NLL against training FLOPs for fixed-size UDLMs with and without looping. These results concern compute efficiency from recurrent depth; they do not evaluate whether loss follows a power law, whether small-run fits extrapolate, or how parameters and tokens should be allocated.
record.test_reason: The study trains one 170M-parameter uniform diffusion LM, with and without looping, on two datasets. It compares training FLOPs needed to reach the baseline's validation NLL. It does not vary parameters, tokens or compute over orders of magnitude, fit power laws, extrapolate, or find compute-optimal splits. Kaplan and Hoffmann are cited only for FLOP-counting conventions (Appendix C).
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that looping makes uniform diffusion LM training more compute-efficient (2.8× fewer FLOPs on OWT, 3.3× on FineWeb-Edu) and improves generation and zero-shot likelihood at inference. They also find that FLOP-proportional loop sampling cuts adaptive loop iterations by 12% without losing accuracy. They draw no scaling-law conclusions.
record.recipe_differences: Studies looping a two-block slice of a UDLM denoiser while keeping its objective and sampler unchanged, rather than fitting loss scaling laws or optimizing parameter/token allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported compute savings differ by dataset and loop-count distribution.

fits_no_version.finding: For a fixed 170M uniform diffusion LM, looping blocks 1–2 reaches the baseline's validation NLL with 2.7–3.3× fewer training FLOPs under Chinchilla counting. Under Kaplan counting the savings are 2.2–2.6×.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Shared-weight looping improves training-FLOP efficiency of uniform diffusion LMs at fixed parameter count; the size of the saving depends on the FLOP-counting convention.

record.problems: The compute-efficiency comparisons are for one stated model size and two datasets, so they do not establish a general scaling relationship. The figure ratios are reported without uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No other results were left out; downstream and generation evaluations do not measure any of the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: All: no power-law fit of loss against parameters, tokens or compute; only one model size.
All: no small-run fits and no extrapolation.
All: no variation of parameter and token counts at fixed compute.
All: the loop-position ablation (Table 5) changes effective depth through weight sharing and adds compute, so it does not hold parameters fixed while varying shape in the sense V4 means.
All: diffusion LM training is not fitted to any power-law form.
All: downstream results are compared across loop policies, not against scale or pretraining loss.
All: no exponents are fitted. The FLOP-convention comparison changes only efficiency ratios, not a scaling law.

record.verdict_notes: Hoffmann and Kaplan are cited only for FLOP-accounting conventions (Appendix C, Figure 9), which is not a use of the scaling-law finding. All rows are the study's own method compared with its baseline at a single model size.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test power-law form, bottleneck conditions, or behavior over several orders of magnitude in parameters, tokens, or compute.
Does not fit small-run laws or test predictions on substantially larger runs.
Does not vary parameter count and token count to identify compute-optimal allocations.
Loop-location ablations do not test the effect of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count as stated in this version.
Does not test scaling-law form across modalities or the listed alternative training regimes.
Reports downstream evaluations across loop policies, not predictability from scale or pretraining loss.
Does not compare scaling-law exponents or fitting choices, or test curve bending away from a power law.

relation.reason: Appendix C cites scaling-law papers for FLOP accounting conventions; the experiments neither test nor rely on a fitted scaling law.

tranche.reason: The study compares looping strategies for one 170M-parameter UDLM architecture. It does not test power-law forms, extrapolation, compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, or another claim version.

source_check.notes: All four ratios are explicitly printed in Figure 1. They describe the study's own method versus its baseline and belong outside scaling-law evidence; the Kaplan ratios in Figure 9 are 2.22, 2.19, 2.61 and 2.59, respectively.
